summary: Bob Thomas's comments on John Day's File Access Protocol proposal in RFC 520. He thinks a protocol of that kind is a good idea, sees its commands as generic file system calls, and suggests mostly additions such as an append mode for opening files.

eli5.summary: A reader liked a plan for using remote files like local ones and suggested extra features, such as adding to the end of a file.

questions: what was the file access protocol
why did rfc 535 suggest file handles
what is a sparse file with holes
subtitle: Suggestions to make remote files work like local ones.

tldr.problem: John Day's File Access Protocol (RFC 520) proposed a way for programs to manipulate files on remote computers using monitor-level calls instead of just transferring whole files. Bob Thomas saw its value but noted it was missing features available to local users, such as appending to files and discovering file structure.
tldr.mechanism: Thomas suggested adding an append mode to the OPEN command, a command to find the next used block in a sparse file, ways to query file metadata and permissions, and file handles to allow simultaneous access to multiple files.
tldr.outcome: The comments represented early thinking about how remote file access should mirror local capabilities, an ideal that influenced decades of file system and remote access protocol design.

today: RFC 535 represents early and thoughtful commentary on remote file access protocol design. The issues Thomas raised—sparse file access, file metadata, simultaneous file handles, and local transformation control—remained central to file system and remote access design for decades.

sections.title: Early Thoughts on Remote File Access
sections.content:
The File Access Protocol (FAP) proposed in RFC 520 by John Day was a step beyond simple file transfer. FTP let users transfer whole files over the network, but FAP aimed to let programs perform file system operations like OPEN, CLOSE, SEEK, and READ on remote files, mirroring the operating system calls available to local programs.

Bob Thomas of BBN-TENEX reviewed the proposal and endorsed the basic idea, but identified several ways the protocol fell short of giving remote users the same capabilities as local users. His comments represented early thinking about how to make network-based file access seamless and complete.
sections.eli5: A programmer said it was a good idea to let programs work with files on other computers using the same commands as local files. A reviewer agreed it was good but said it was missing some important things.

sections.title: Missing Features: Append, Structure Discovery, and Metadata
sections.content:
Thomas noted that FAP did not support append mode, even though many systems (like TENEX) allow users to append to a file without having write permission. He suggested adding an OPEN A (append) mode that would seek to the end of the file before writing.

FAP also lacked a way to discover file structure. On TENEX, files can have "holes" (gaps of unallocated space), and a remote user could not know where these holes are without prior knowledge. Thomas proposed a new command, FNUB (Find Next Used Block), that would return the file pointer position of the next allocated block, allowing remote programs to navigate sparse files as local programs do.

The protocol did not provide file metadata—access permissions, size information, creation and modification dates, or per-page access control. Thomas suggested these be retrievable so remote users could make informed decisions about access and use.
sections.eli5: You should be able to add to the end of a file, find out where the empty spaces are in a file, and ask what the file's size and permissions are—things local programs could always do.

sections.title: File Handles and Multiple Simultaneous Access
sections.content:
FAP as proposed allowed only one file to be open at a time. Thomas suggested introducing file handles (server-chosen identifiers like a string or small integer) that would be returned by OPEN and used in subsequent commands. This would let a user open and work with multiple files simultaneously, a common need for local programs.

With file handles, a sequence like OPEN R FOO, OPEN W MOO, READ 3 FH, WRITE 2 MH would become straightforward. Reasonable defaults could make handles optional: for instance, a command without a handle could default to the file opened in the previous command, reducing the overhead on the protocol.
sections.eli5: Let programs open and work with more than one file at the same time, the way they can on real computers, by giving each file a number or name to refer to it by.

sections.title: Local Transformation Control
sections.content:
RFC 520 mentioned the importance of accounting for local file transformations (such as TENEX converting line endings). Thomas agreed that transformation was important for compatibility, but remote programs should also be able to suppress transformations when desired, so they could access the underlying file bytes directly if needed.

This flexibility would allow the same program logic to work whether operating on files locally (with direct system calls) or remotely (with FAP commands relayed to a remote site), an ideal of seamless transparent access.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the network might change line endings in text files automatically, but a program should be able to say "send me the raw file exactly as stored" when it needs that.

references.text: Day, J. D., "File Access Protocol", RFC 520, June 13, 1973.
